body_en:
A cold or a fever costs almost nothing. But one serious illness is enough to bankrupt a family. On social media, pleas from families driven into poverty by illness — or forced to give up treatment — are everywhere.

Health Insurance with No Out-of-Pocket Cap

China's health insurance system has no cap on what a patient pays out of pocket — in other words, there is no upper limit on how much a patient might have to pay in a year.

By comparison, the out-of-pocket maximum is around $9,000 in the United States and about ¥530,000 in Japan. Both figures are roughly two to three months' wages for an average salaried worker there. Anything beyond the cap is covered by insurance.

With no cap, drug prices can smash straight through what a family can afford. Take the drug in the photo below: dinutuximab beta injection. It used to cost ¥59,500 a vial; after being added to the insurance list, it's ¥6,000 a vial — and even so, six months of treatment still costs ¥150,000.

Being on the Insurance List Doesn't Mean It's Covered

Human albumin is a common drug in cancer treatment — about ¥750 a vial, one vial a day, more than ¥20,000 a month.

The same drug gets very different treatment under different types of insurance: publicly funded medical care covers it, while employee health insurance does not.

And being on the insurance list doesn't guarantee reimbursement either. Human albumin is a Class B drug, which in principle employee insurance can reimburse at up to 90% — but in practice, cancer patients often have to pay for it themselves.

Targeted Drugs: ¥100,000 a Month

Take the targeted drugs bevacizumab and cetuximab: about ¥100,000 a month.

Both now have generic versions, and both are on the insurance list. But being listed doesn't mean they're reimbursed: gastric cancer isn't within their approved indications, so it's still not covered. At current prices, six months on the cheaper generic costs ¥110,000; the original brand-name drug costs ¥160,000.

Even a Pension, Savings, and Extra Insurance Aren't Enough

Even families with a pension, savings, and employer-provided supplemental commercial insurance struggle with drug bills of tens of thousands of yuan a month, and can only cut back on medication.

For a farming family living on a ¥200 monthly pension, cancer is almost entirely beyond their means. The rural cooperative insurance reimburses far less than employee insurance, and the gap in coverage is even wider.

Rare Diseases: Lifelong Treatment at ¥100,000 a Month

For patients with rare diseases, the situation is more extreme still. Pompe disease, for example, requires lifelong treatment at ¥100,000 a month. Even after insurance reimbursement, the remaining cost is beyond what an ordinary family can bear.

A serious illness first drains the savings, then drains a family's future. And with no out-of-pocket cap in health insurance, there is no floor to that hole.
excerpt_en: A cold costs almost nothing, but one serious illness can bankrupt a family. In China, health insurance has no out-of-pocket cap — and that open-ended gap can swallow everything a family has.
title_en: How Much Does a Serious Illness Cost?
